title: Your own data
text: The published session description invited you to bring messy historical datasets. An hour is not enough to work on them together, but the sequence transfers. Here is how to start, in the order that worked for the Tropical and Imperial Careers projects.

title: Your own data
text:
Before you open a model

Pick one question and one small sample. Twenty records you can check by hand beat two thousand you cannot. The sample should include at least one hard case.
Keep the source reachable. Every record needs a reference that gets a reader back to the page: file, page, line or offset. If your text came from OCR, keep the page images available. You will need them.
Decide what a record is. A person? A mention of a person? An event? The Tropical project’s “863 records” for Trimen are chunk-level extractions, not occurrences, and that distinction mattered later.

title: Your own data
text:
The sequence








Step
Ask the model to
You




Structure
Read the sample and propose fields, with two example records
Decide what the question requires and what the source can support


Extract
Process the sample, keep printed wording, put inferences in separate fields, save code and outputs, report failures
Inspect for omissions, invented details and changed meaning


Candidates
Retrieve identities with a verifiable lookup, save the evidence and the date
Judge whether the identity fits the historical context


Review
Build a side-by-side evidence table with accept / reject / unresolved and a reason field
Decide, and write the reason


Revise
Find other records with the same problem, propose a fix, rerun the sample, show what changed
Check the fix and look for new errors before scaling up



The draft prompts on step 2 are a starting point. Adapt the nouns.

title: Your own data
section: Rules that saved the research projects trouble
text:
Rules that saved the research projects trouble

Local identifiers first. Give every record a stable local id before any external identifier. Add a Wikidata link only after retrieval and review support it. If nothing suitable exists, keep the local id; do not invent one.
No identifiers from memory. A model will offer plausible Q-numbers. Treat any identifier that was not retrieved by a tool as unverified. The earlier workshop has a longer note on this.
Separate structuring from grounding, and both from modern classification. A plant name in 1883 is a historical usage; what Kew calls that plant today is a separate record.
Model decisions and human decisions in different columns. Never overwrite the one with the other. The Tropical review page exports the human decisions with a dataset fingerprint so they cannot be attached to the wrong version of the data.
Make the correction a test. When a review finds a defect, the probe that found it becomes a regression test. Tropical’s three name probes are now in its test suite.
Report what the sample can support. Handpicked cases explain failure modes. A stratified sample measures precision for one stratum. Neither measures recall.

title: Your own data
section: Tools, and what they cost at scale
text:
Tools, and what they cost at scale
Two different jobs need two different kinds of model.

The agent that writes the pipeline reads your sample, proposes the structure, writes and tests the script, and builds the review view. This is a few hours of a frontier model’s time per project. The saved runs A and B used Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 in Claude Code.
The model inside the pipeline reads every chunk of the collection. At tens of thousands of articles the frontier models are too expensive. The Tropical project’s extraction over 53,000 articles used Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 served by vLLM on a shared university GPU, and run C in outputs/02-extract/ is the same model on the same two passages, so you can compare what the cheap model does with the same prompts.

The agent can write the pipeline so that the cheap model does the reading and the agent is only called back when something fails. Which operation produced a given record should remain visible in the output.
The presenter’s environment uses Claude Code as the coding agent and the WikidataMCP server for lookups. Any coding agent that can run code, read files and call a lookup tool will do. See Run it yourself for the setup used here, and for what is still to be confirmed about costs.

title: Further: what a correction becomes
text: The review has produced a decision with a reason. The reason is the valuable part: it tells the model what class of error to look for. The prompt:

title: Further: what a correction becomes
text:
Two revisions that actually happened
Both are in outputs/05-revise/README.md. They were not staged for the workshop; they are what the research projects did on 6 October 2026.
A safeguard that validated invented names. Tropical’s profile builder accepted a printed initial as proof that a full given name was “in the article”. Three probes against the old code accepted James Watt for Mr. J. Watt, Henry Trimen for Mr. H. Trimen, and John Smith for Mr. John Smithson. The historian’s reason: a model that knows who “F. von Mueller” probably is has added outside knowledge to the record, and that must be kept apart from what the source prints. The fix returns a status instead of a yes: full, initials or none. Across the corpus, 889 expansions moved from “verified” to “hypothesis”. The three probes became regression tests.
A mixed profile is not one person. The merge that built the authority table was supposed to leave the identifier empty when a model judged a profile MIXED. A fallback filled it anyway from the Colonial Office List. Two profiles that the model had explicitly called two people left the pipeline with one identifier each at “high” confidence. The fix is a single identity gate that says what a profile may assert and what remains a candidate, with tests that name the two cases.
And one from this packet. The exercise letter’s OCR was wrong in two sentences. The extraction model flagged both as uncertain and then guessed at the intended wording. Both guesses were wrong. The rule that follows: an uncertain reading is not data until someone has looked at the page, and a model’s guess is not a reading.

title: Further: what a correction becomes
section: What to check after a revision
text:
What to check after a revision

The cases the change was meant to fix.
The previously accepted cases that changed. In the Tropical v2 rebuild this was the larger group.
Whether the new rule is now a test, so the error cannot come back when the code is next edited.

A model can do all three of these checks. Deciding that the original result was wrong, and why, was the historian’s work.

title: Further: what a correction becomes
section: What a second model can and cannot do
text:
What a second model can and cannot do
A second model can review the first model’s output and find problems. Its agreement is not historical confirmation: two models reading the editor’s headnote will agree with the editor. Review a mixture of uncertain cases and apparently successful ones. Handpicked workshop cases explain failure modes; they do not establish an accuracy rate.
Next: Connecting collections.

title: Ground
text:
Records now have local identifiers (henry, agar, illustrated_tree). The next step proposes external identities for the people, so that this small dataset can connect to the Colonial Office List graph and to anything else that uses Wikidata identifiers.
Two sources of candidates:

title: Ground
text:
The prompt

Look up candidate identities for these people using the configured Wikidata tools and the supplied Colonial Office List records. Save the retrieved evidence and lookup date. For each candidate, show what supports the match, what conflicts, and what is missing. Leave unresolved cases unresolved. Do not generate QIDs from memory.

title: Ground
text:
Three questions to keep separate

Does the identifier resolve to the retrieved entity? We only show QIDs we fetched. A Q-number supplied from a model’s memory is not a lookup.
Is that entity the one described in this source? Name, type, dates, geography, activity. A real item can still be the wrong person.
What does the connection assert? Linking “Dr. Trimen” in S04 to Q2462643 asserts that this mention refers to that man. It does not assert that every statement on the Wikidata item is true, or that the 1883 “Ceylon” is the modern state.

Keep the evidence for each match. Record unresolved cases as unresolved, with the searches that were run, so that nobody repeats them or mistakes “not found” for “does not exist”.
Next: Clean, together.

title: The page
section: Take the question to an unstructured collection
text:
Take the question to an unstructured collection
The Tropical Agriculturist (Colombo, from 1881) printed reports, letters and reprints for the planting community. The Tropical Agriculturist project has OCR text for about 53,500 articles. A search for articles mentioning both “Trimen” and “Howard” returns 72 of them. That is a discovery set, not 72 relationships.
Our question for the hour:

Who is Henry Trimen connected to in The Tropical Agriculturist, and what evidence supports those connections?

We will work with a handful of items from 1883, when the journal ran a dispute it headlined “The Wars of the Quinologists”:



Id
Item
Why it is here




S02
“The Wars of the Quinologists”, July 1883, pp. 27–28
The editor frames a dispute among Howard, Trimen and Moens


S03
“Dr. Trimen’s Ledgeriana: Mr. T. N. Christie to the Rescue”, July 1883, p. 37
A planter traces the illustrated tree’s seed and nursery


S04
“Dr. Trimen’s Typical Ledgeriana Tree”, July 1883, p. 66
Walter Agar’s 234-word letter. The exercise passage.


S05, S06
“The Cinchona Calisaya (or Ledgeriana) Discussion” and “The Botany of Cinchona Ledgeriana”, December 1883, pp. 453–455
Trimen’s reply, signed from Peradeniya, with the competing identifications


S01
“Mr. Eliot Howard Extinguishing C. Pubescentis How.”, July 1881, pp. 114–115
Optional: Howard rejects a species name credited to him



We begin after OCR. Other sessions cover OCR production. The page images stay one click away, and you will need them.

title: The page
text:
Ten years ago
The problems in this hour are not new. Trading Consequences (2012–2013) text-mined 10.5 million scanned pages of nineteenth-century British sources for commodities, places and dates: historians at Saskatchewan and York, computational linguists at Edinburgh, a database team at EDINA, visualisation at St Andrews, funded by Digging into Data. The write-up is Clifford, Alex, Coates, Klein and Watson, “Geoparsing history: Locating commodities in ten million pages of nineteenth-century sources”, Historical Methods 49:3 (2016), 115–131, doi:10.1080/01615440.2015.1116419. Its difficulties are the same three we will work on, at a scale and cost that is worth remembering:









Trading Consequences, 2013
This hour




Cleaning
OCR turned “lime” into “time” and “line”, long-s “salt” into “fait”; tables collapsed into 210-word “sentences” that linked “glass, glue and gelatine” to every country in a trade return. Fixes were hand-built: a hyphenation joiner, an f-to-s lexicon, a filter for table-heavy documents. 14.9% of locations in the gold standard contained OCR errors.
Two sentences of a 234-word letter are wrong in the OCR, in ways that reverse the meaning. The model flags them; the page settles them (case R3).


Structuring
A six-stage pipeline (format conversion, OCR post-correction, linguistic pre-processing, named-entity recognition, attribute recognition, relation extraction), adapted from the Edinburgh Geoparser by computational linguists. A relation was “same sentence”. A commodity lexicon had to be bootstrapped from customs records and Wikipedia because no expert list existed.
The coding agent proposes the fields, writes the script and reports failures in minutes (step 2). The historian still decides what a record is.


Grounding
GeoNames string matching with geographic coherence scoring. “Saharunpore” was not found because the gazetteer only knew “Saharanpur”; “British West India Islands” grounded to West India; a bug placed every “Italy” in a Texan town. Final F-scores: 0.62 for commodities, 0.61 for locations. Two trained annotators agreed on what counted as a commodity only 72% of the time.
Semantic search over Wikidata plus statement reading, cached with timestamps (step 3). Walter Agar still is not there (case R4). Entities absent from the authority, and plausible wrong matches, are the same problem with a better search box.


Review
Historians spotted false positives through the visualisations (“Saumur” as a place in a wine list); false negatives were invisible. A gold standard of double-annotated documents measured precision and recall.
Same two lessons: errors you can see get fixed, errors you cannot see need a sample; and a corrected error should become a rule (step 5).



What changed is who writes the pipeline and how fast the loop from error to fix runs. What did not change is where historical judgment is needed. The paper’s closing advice to historians, that they should build the lexicons, gazetteers and structured data that software developers will not, is the premise of the exercise.

title: The page
Run it yourself
text:
To be confirmed before the session



The exact agent, model and lookup configuration to be demonstrated has not been fixed yet, and the costs of running the example with a personal account have not been measured. This page describes the configuration used to prepare the materials.

title: Run it yourself
text:
What is in the repository
source-pack/          OCR text, scan-checked transcription, Colonial Office List entries, citations
outputs/01-structure/ model proposals for the record structure (one folder per run)
outputs/02-extract/   extraction scripts, records and notes (one folder per run)
outputs/03-candidates/ candidate identities with retrieved evidence
outputs/05-revise/    the two real revisions, with before and after
outputs/06-connect/   Trimen across the three collections
review/               the browser exercise (static HTML + cases.json)
research/trimen-network/  the wider research packet and the cached Wikidata responses
scripts/              build scripts (no network needed except ground_trimen.py)

title: Run it yourself
text:
Rerunning the saved extraction
Each extraction run saved a script that regenerates its records from the OCR text, offline:
python3 outputs/02-extract/run-A/02_extract.py source-pack

title: Run it yourself
text:
Rebuilding the tables
python3 scripts/build_trimen_workshop.py   # research packet CSV/JSON from the frozen search extract
python3 scripts/build_candidates.py        # candidate evidence from the cached Wikidata responses
python3 scripts/build_source_pack.py       # participant source pack
python3 scripts/build_review_cases.py      # cases.json for the exercise
None of these touch the network.

title: Run it yourself
section: Running the extraction with a local open model
text:
Running the extraction with a local open model
outputs/02-extract/run-C/02_extract.py sends the two prompts to any OpenAI-compatible server (the saved run used Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 under vLLM on the University of Saskatchewan’s Plato cluster; scripts/plato_qwen_extract.slurm is the job). Point it at your own server:
python3 outputs/02-extract/run-C/02_extract.py --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 --model <served-name> --sources source-pack --out /tmp/runC
The model in this mode is not an agent: it returns the records as JSON and the script saves them. That is the shape of a production pipeline, where the agent writes the script once and the cheap model runs inside it.

title: Run it yourself
section: Running the live steps with your own agent
text:
Running the live steps with your own agent
You need a coding agent that can read files, run Python and call a Wikidata lookup tool. The materials were prepared with Claude Code and the WikidataMCP server (Streamable HTTP endpoint https://wd-mcp.wmcloud.org/mcp). Two things to know:

Use the vector search, not the string search. Wikidata’s ordinary search API matches labels by string similarity. “Walpole Island” returns an island in New Caledonia. The MCP server’s search_items uses semantic embeddings. It is rate limited; cache what you retrieve.
No identifiers from memory. Tell the agent, and check its output. The research packet’s scripts/ground_trimen.py shows one way to cache full entity responses with retrieval timestamps.

To fetch fresh evidence for an entity:
python3 scripts/ground_trimen.py entities Q2462643
python3 scripts/ground_trimen.py search "Walter Agar Ceylon planter"

title: Run it yourself
text:
Credentials
No file in this repository contains a credential, and none is needed for the exercise. If you configure an agent with an API key, keep it out of the repository.

title: Research packet: the Trimen network
text: The tables below live in research/trimen-network/: entities.csv, claims.csv, letters.csv, taxonomy.csv, archival-leads.csv, with JSON equivalents, the seven frozen article records in sources/, and the cached Wikidata responses in raw/. The packet’s own description follows.

title: Research packet: the Trimen network
text:
The passages to use
Seven frozen article records are in sources/. Each retains the Tropical article ID, OCR text, page links, and source segments. The July 1883 opening on scan n44 has been visually inspected. Other passages have been read in OCR and still need comparison with their scans before presenting a final transcription. The parent search file contains 72 articles with both surnames; that is a discovery set, not 72 verified relationships between Henry Trimen and John Eliot Howard.



Source
Passage
Why it matters




S01
“Mr. Eliot Howard Extinguishing C. Pubescentis How.”, July 1881, pp. 114–115
Howard disclaims having created a species under this name. The editorial also criticizes Clements Markham’s account of hybrid parentage.


S02
“The Wars of the Quinologists”, July 1883, pp. 27–28
The journal explicitly presents a dispute among Howard, Trimen, and Moens. A short opening for the workshop.


S03
“Dr. Trimen’s Ledgeriana: Mr. T. N. Christie to the Rescue”, p. 37
Christie’s letter of 7 June 1883 traces the illustrated plant through McIvor’s seed, his nursery, and Agar’s planting. This is Christie’s asserted provenance.


S04
“Dr. Trimen’s Typical Ledgeriana Tree”, p. 66
Agar’s letter of 22 June 1883 distinguishes the illustrated tree from other trees whose bark Campbell sent to Howard. Excellent material for checking a model’s proposed relationship.


S05
“The Cinchona Calisaya (or Ledgeriana) Discussion”, December 1883, p. 453
Howard’s quoted letter and Trimen’s cover letter connect people, publications and places. Trimen writes from Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya on 21 November.


S06
“The Botany of Cinchona Ledgeriana”, December 1883, pp. 453–455
Trimen’s argument, dated 29 October, reports competing identifications and distinguishes botanical characters from chemical yield.


S07
“History of Cinchona Culture in Ceylon”, April–June 1943, beginning p. 91
A retrospective account brings in Markham, Spruce, plant movements, Peradeniya and Hakgala. Publication date must remain separate from the events described.



The direct Trimen–Howard connection is a published disagreement, not merely article co-occurrence. Trimen’s reply goes to the editor of the Pharmaceutical Journal and is forwarded for publication in Ceylon; it should not be recoded as a private letter addressed to Howard.

title: Research packet: the Trimen network
text:
Grounding people, plants and places
entities.csv and entities.json contain 49 local entities, with candidate QIDs where authority records have been checked. record_checked means that the Wikidata item was retrieved and examined. It does not mean that every historical occurrence of that name has been matched, that every statement on the item is trustworthy, or that a human has approved the proposal. Every human-review field remains pending.
The people include Henry Trimen (Q2462643), John Eliot Howard (Q3181423), Clements Markham (Q507802), Moens (Q21340893), McIvor (Q21520254), Charles Ledger (Q963818), Weddell (Q983408), Joseph Dalton Hooker (Q157501), Fitch (Q1102060), and Richard Spruce (Q1349394). The correspondence adds Roland Trimen (Q932702), Thiselton-Dyer (Q2065240), and Daniel Morris (Q20733957). Surname-only assignments remain proposals supported by context.
Thomas North Christie and Walter Agar retain local identifiers. No suitable Wikidata match was established in the searches performed. Absence from those results does not demonstrate that an item does not exist. Christie must not be merged with Thomas Christy on spelling similarity. Moens’s cached authority labels and aliases disagree about his given name, so the packet retains initials. Trimen’s account also mentions an unnamed servant of Ledger; keeping a local record prevents that person’s involvement from disappearing merely because the source supplies no personal name.
Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya (Q3119056) is explicit in the 1883 cover letter. Peradeniya as a locality has a separate candidate, Q489744. Likewise, Kew’s garden site and the research institution have distinct items. The bare word Hakgala in a catalogue address does not establish that the sender was inside the botanical garden. Estates such as St. Andrew’s, Mahanillu and Yarrow remain local records without invented coordinates.
Howards and Sons (Q123413890) provides a possible industrial branch. The archive catalogue for collection ACC/1037 describes the firm’s pharmaceutical business and its Stratford headquarters before the move to Ilford. This is external contextual evidence, kept distinct from the Tropical passages. Howards and Sons archive catalogue
West Ham is a useful correction to a model’s reasoning. The label “County Borough of West Ham” initially suggested that Q5177625 would be too late for the 1883 setting. Jim pointed out that the item includes the local board of health. Its statements explicitly cover that form from 1856 to 1886. The packet therefore retains the QID for West Ham local government, with the appropriate period and label. The county-borough start qualifier currently says 1 April 1899, while the municipal-borough end says 31 March 1889; these unreferenced statements require investigation. Accepting an identity link does not require accepting all attached dates. Wikidata record

title: Research packet: the Trimen network
section: Historical classification is part of the evidence
text:
Historical classification is part of the evidence
Some historical identifications may have been wrong. The data must preserve enough detail to examine that question: who identified which plant, under what name, when, and on what evidence? Trimen’s claim that several differently named plants were botanically identical belongs in the dataset as his argument, rather than as an automatic correction to all earlier records.
claims.csv and claims.json contain 14 proposed relationships with exact OCR evidence, attribution and review notes. The illustrated tree and its neighbouring trees have separate local IDs. Agar says that bark from some trees went to Howard, while bark from the illustrated tree remained in his possession. An extraction that says Howard analysed the illustrated tree would overstate the evidence. The source’s word “typical” also does not by itself establish nomenclatural type status.
There are three separate questions to retain:

Which name did a historical actor use?
Which specimen or group of plants did that actor identify with that name?
How does a current authority treat the name?

Kew’s Plants of the World Online currently treats Cinchona ledgeriana as a synonym of C. calisaya, and C. succirubra as a synonym of C. pubescens. These treatments are recorded separately in taxonomy.csv; they do not settle whether Howard or Trimen correctly identified a particular historical tree. Ledgeriana record, succirubra record
The 1881 Howard letter makes an especially useful case. It distinguishes a hybrid that people were calling “C. pubescens How.” from an already established species with different characters. Mapping both occurrences directly to Q164574 would erase the issue the letter discusses. A separate local historical-name record preserves it.
Bark, cinchona alkaloids and quinine also have separate records. Pure quinine and sulphate of quinine are not interchangeable measurements. The packet includes only a selection of the plant names Jim supplied; unexamined species, categories and taxonomy templates have not been inserted as if they were all participants in this dispute.

title: Research packet: the Trimen network
section: Correspondence as the next research branch
text:
Correspondence as the next research branch
letters.csv and letters.json transcribe 25 distinct catalogue entries supplied by Jim, spanning 1893–1896. Repeated display titles in the pasted list have been collapsed. There are 24 letters attributed to Henry: 23 to Thiselton-Dyer and one to Daniel Morris. One is attributed to Roland Trimen, writing to Thiselton-Dyer from 5 Lancaster Street on 31 December 1896.
These records establish catalogue-described correspondence, dates, origins, folios, and page/image counts. They do not establish what the letters discuss. The list is a selection, not a complete correspondence census. Repository URLs for individual entries have not yet been matched.
Jim also supplied kdcas1413 and kdcas1411. These are retained separately in archival-leads.csv. The records could not be retrieved during this check; their subjects and correspondence dates remain unverified. No association has been inferred from their sequential identifiers.
For the workshop, show this branch briefly as the next question opened by the research. Reading a whole correspondence collection belongs in the follow-up materials, not the hour’s core exercise.

title: Research packet: the Trimen network
text:
Reuse and remaining preparation
Run python3 scripts/build_trimen_workshop.py from the workshop repository to rebuild the CSV and JSON files. It validates exact evidence strings, referenced local entities, unique correspondence IDs, and the presence of cached candidate authority records. manifest.json records the hash of the frozen search input. The public retrieval helper, scripts/ground_trimen.py, caches full Wikidata responses under raw/, including qualifiers, references and retrieval timestamps.
Before presenting, compare the selected exercise passage with its scan, review the proposed identities and claims, and attach a small Colonial Office List excerpt for Henry’s career. Keep the broader research packet available on GitHub, but limit the participant exercise to a short passage and a few decisions. The packet is saved locally; this workspace is not yet a Git repository and nothing has been published.

title: Worked answers
text: These are the preparer’s answers with the evidence. They are not the research project’s verdicts: every human-review field in the Tropical pipeline and in the research packet is still pending, and these pages do not change that.

title: Worked answers
section: R3 (Clean). The OCR reading does not stand
text:
R3 (Clean). The OCR reading does not stand
Reject the reading. The scan of p. 66 reads: “The trees were only about 4½ years old from the time the plants were put out, and were growing in a bad situation and not robust.” The OCR’s “were now in a full condition and in flower” is an invention of the OCR model, not a misread of a few characters. The next sentence is also wrong in the OCR: the scan reads “I have many plants from the seed of the specimen tree as well as the others that Mr. Moens declared to be true Ledgerianas”, not “prints of the leaves”.
Both extraction runs flagged these sentences as uncertain. Both guessed at the intended wording. All the guesses were wrong. The flag was the useful output; the page was the only way to resolve it.
The corrected transcription is in the source pack with the list of differences.

title: Worked answers
section: R2 (Structure). Howard did not analyse the illustrated tree’s bark
text:
R2 (Structure). Howard did not analyse the illustrated tree’s bark
Reject the relationship as proposed. Agar’s letter is explicit twice over. The bark Howard analysed came from “some of these trees”, the group at Mahanilu that Moens and Trimen saw in flower. The bark of “the tree itself” is in Agar’s possession, “taken when it was dying”, and no analysis of it is mentioned. The editor’s headnote, which says Howard gave testimony “after having analyzed the bark” of the figured tree, is the editor’s summary and it overstates the letter.
The correct records are two: Howard analysed bark from the neighbouring trees (asserted by Agar); Agar holds bark from the illustrated tree (asserted by Agar). The research packet has them as claims C09, C10 and C11.
Why it is consequential: the dispute was whether that tree was a true Ledgeriana. If the dataset says Howard’s 7 per cent quinine result belongs to it, the dataset has settled the dispute on evidence that does not exist. Christie’s letter (S03) makes a related but different claim: the figured tree and the analysed trees were raised from the same seed in the same nursery bed. That is an argument from provenance, and it is Christie’s.
What remains open: whether “some of these trees” included the figured tree is not stated. Agar’s wording (“the bark from the tree itself” set against “the bark of some of these trees”) implies not, but does not say so.

title: Worked answers
text:
R1 (Ground). “Dr. Trimen” / “HENRY TRIMEN” is Q2462643
Accept, for the 1883 mentions signed from Peradeniya. The December 1883 cover letter is signed in full and dated from the Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya. The Colonial Office List has one Henry Trimen, director of the Royal Botanical Gardens, Ceylon, from February 1880. The Wikidata item, retrieved and read, is a botanist born 1843, died 1896. The name, post, place and dates agree.
What the acceptance covers: these mentions. It does not by itself cover every “Trimen” in the journal. Roland Trimen, Henry’s brother, is in both collections too, and the Tropical pipeline found two more “Trimens” who turned out to be OCR errors for Howard and Ledger (step 6). A supported identity is a decision about a mention, made on evidence that would not transfer to “Mr. Trimen” in a different year.

title: Worked answers
section: R4 (Ground). Walter Agar: unresolved, keep the local record
text:
R4 (Ground). Walter Agar: unresolved, keep the local record
Unresolved. Two vector searches, one with the name alone and one with “Ceylon planter”, returned nothing plausible: a politician named Sarger, the Agar family name, a zoologist born in 1882, a temple, a thickening agent. The right outcome is a local record agar with its evidence (the signature, the dateline “Lawrence”, the role in the Mahanilu planting) and a note of the searches run and their date, so that the next person does not repeat them or read “no result” as “no such person”.
What would resolve it: a Ceylon directory or planters’ register entry for an Agar at Lawrence or Mahanilu in the early 1880s. The research pipeline has a planters’ registry match stage for exactly this.

title: Worked answers
section: R5 (Ground, extra). “C. pubescens How.” is not simply Q164574
text:
R5 (Ground, extra). “C. pubescens How.” is not simply Q164574
Reject the link as a plain identity; record a historical name usage. Howard’s 1881 letter says he is “credited with having created a new species of Cinchona, the ‘C. pubescens How.’” and goes on to reject the attribution: the plants so named are, in his view, something else. Mapping the string to the accepted species Cinchona pubescens records the opposite of what the letter says. The research packet keeps a separate record, pubescens_how, for the rejected usage, alongside the taxon name record for the accepted species.
Modern taxonomy is a separate layer again: Kew’s Plants of the World Online currently treats C. succirubra as a synonym of C. pubescens and C. ledgeriana as a synonym of C. calisaya. Those treatments are recorded in the packet’s taxonomy table with their date. They do not settle what Howard, Trimen or Moens meant by a name in 1883, nor which tree was which.

title: Worked answers
section: R6 (Ground, extra). “Mr. T. Christy” and “Thos. North Christie” are different people
text:
R6 (Ground, extra). “Mr. T. Christy” and “Thos. North Christie” are different people
Reject the merge. The author writes about “Mr. T. Christy’s Bolivian calisaya seedlings” in the third person and criticises Howard for identifying them as Ledgerianas. The author signs “THOS. NORTH CHRISTIE” from an estate in Maskeliya; the Christy seedlings are Bolivian and reach Howard in England. One letter of spelling distance is well within OCR error, which is why this case exists: spelling similarity would merge them, and the text keeps them apart.
Both extraction runs kept them separate without being told to. Run B supplied, from memory and marked unverified, “Thomas Christy, London drug merchant” for Mr. T. Christy. That is a plausible candidate and it is not evidence; the searches run on 6 October found no Wikidata item for either man.

title: Worked answers
text:
The pattern
Across the six cases the decisive evidence was never the model’s confidence and never the identifier’s existence. It was the source’s own distinctions (some trees versus the tree itself; Christy versus Christie; a name credited versus a name claimed), the page behind the OCR, and the dates and posts in a second collection. Those are what the review view has to put in front of you, and what the reason field is for.

title: Presenter notes
section: The two decisions to make together
text:
The two decisions to make together
The editor’s bracketed note above Agar’s letter says that Howard “analyzed the bark” of the tree Trimen figured. Agar’s letter says that bark from some of these trees went to Howard, and that the bark from the tree itself is in Agar’s own possession. A model that follows the editor conflates the two. Neither rehearsal run did: run A recorded the editor’s claim as the editor’s and noted that which trees supplied the bark “is not stated beyond ‘some of these trees’”; run B noted on the editor’s affirmation that Agar only says the figured tree was “one of several”. Show run A’s bark record and ask the room whether they would have caught it if the model had not. If a live run in the room does conflate them, better still.
Then the OCR check: both runs flagged the two damaged sentences and guessed at the wording (run A “in full bloom”; both runs “by me”). The scan says “growing in a bad situation and not robust” and “many plants from the seed of the specimen tree”. The models were right to flag and wrong to guess.

title: Cleaning, Structuring and Grounding Historical Data
text:
You: supported, unresolved, or wrong

Does the identifier resolve to what was retrieved? A Q-number from a model’s memory is not a lookup.
Is that entity the one in this source? Name, type, dates, place, activity. A real item can be the wrong person.
What does the link assert? This mention is that man. Not every statement on the item. Not that 1883 “Ceylon” is the modern state.


Trimen: supported, for these mentions. Agar: unresolved; keep the local record and the searches that were run. “Not found” is not “does not exist”.

Chandra 2, a vision-language OCR model. Tested on this corpus; good results. In the production corpus, this page:

… were put out, and were now in a full condition and in flower.

The page:

title: Cleaning, Structuring and Grounding Historical Data
section: OCR is better, and not perfect
text:
OCR is better, and not perfect
The old archive.org text layer, same sentences:

… ami were growing; in a bad situation and not robust. I have many plants from the seed of the specimen^ tree as well as the oiheis that Mr. Moens declared …



The old OCR’s errors look like errors. The new OCR’s errors read like prose.
The two frontier runs flagged the sentences, then guessed; every guess was wrong. The affordable model reported the sentence as fact.
The two OCRs disagree exactly where the new one is wrong.
Re-run on the page image alone, Chandra reads both sentences correctly, three times out of three. The error belongs to the production run, not the model. Nothing in the text tells you which you got.

A model can tell you a sentence reads oddly. Only the page tells you what it says.

title: Cleaning, Structuring and Grounding Historical Data
text:
What the correction becomes

This example is wrong for the following reason: [explain]. Find other records that might have the same problem. Propose a correction and show which records it would affect. Rerun a small batch and show both corrected cases and previously accepted cases that changed.



An uncertain reading is not data until someone has looked at the page.
A model’s guess at the wording is not a reading.
Where two OCRs disagree, send the sentence to a human.
The probe that found the error becomes a test.


If there is time: the Tropical name-evidence fix (initial accepted as full name; 889 “verified” expansions became hypotheses; three probes now tests). Otherwise point to the Further pages.

title: Structure
text:
Walter Agar’s letter, printed under the editor’s headline “Dr. Trimen’s Typical Ledgeriana Tree” on 2 July 1883, p. 66 (scan). The OCR text, exactly as the collection delivers it:
DR. TRIMEN'S TYPICAL LEDGERIANA TREE.

[We publish below a letter from Mr. Agar, which places beyond question the fact that the tree figured by Dr. Trimen was an undoubted Ledgeriana, Mr. Howard himself having given testimony to that effect after having analyzed the bark.—Ed.]

Lawrence, June 22nd, 1883.

DEAR SIR,—I have little to add to what Mr. Christie has written on the subject of Ledgerianas, but that little is, I think, important.

The tree, which was sketched for Dr. Trimen's work, is dead.

It was one of several Mr. Moens saw in flower at Mahanillu estate, Dr. Trimen was with Mr. Moens, and both agreed the trees were true Ledgerianas. The bark of some of these trees was sent home by Mr. Campbell for analysis to Mr. Howard, who pronounced it to be Ledgeriana bark, giving 7 per cent of pure quinine (equal I believe to 9 of sulphate) and only a trace of other alkaloids. The trees were only about 4½ years old from the time the plants were put out, and were now in a full condition and in flower.

I have by my prints of the leaves of some of the trees as well as the other that Mr. Moens had sent to be true Ledgerianas, so that it will be easy in the future to determine the question.

I have also in my possession the bark from the tree itself, but taken when it was dying.—Yours truly,

WALTER AGAR.

Two hundred and thirty-four words. People, a tree, a group of trees, bark samples, an analysis, and a chain of hands. Also a headnote by the editor saying what the letter proves.

title: Structure
text:
The prompts
Two prompts, used verbatim in the saved runs. They are starting points, not tested final instructions.
Propose a structure

Read these Tropical Agriculturist passages. Propose a small table for studying the people and activities mentioned. Show two example records before processing the rest. Preserve the printed wording and source references. Keep inferred information separate from what the text states. Use local record identifiers and do not add Wikidata identifiers yet.

Build and run the extraction

Use the agreed fields to process this sample. Save the code, instructions, and output so we can inspect and rerun the work. Report failed records and uncertain readings. Do not expand a person’s name unless the source provides the expansion; record any outside identification separately.

Note what the prompts ask for beyond the records: two examples before the rest, so the structure can be corrected cheaply; saved code so the run can be repeated and inspected; a report of failures; and a wall between what the source prints and what the model knows.

title: Structure
text:
What to inspect
Three things, in this order, before anything else is built on the records:

Omissions. Is everyone and everything in the passage in the table? Both runs have “Ed.” as a person record, which is right: the editor makes claims.
Invented details. Did a name get a given name the text does not print? Did a relative date become an absolute one without saying so? Run B resolved “5th instant” to 5 June 1883 and said so in the inferred field. Run B also filled an outside_identification field for six people from its own memory, each marked UNVERIFIED. That is the behaviour the prompt asked for; the next step replaces memory with retrieval.
Changed meaning. Did a careful statement become a flat one? The editor says Howard analysed “the bark” of the figured tree. Agar says bark from some trees went to Howard and the figured tree’s bark is in his own drawer. Both runs kept these apart. Would a third?

And one thing none of the runs could do: two sentences of the OCR are damaged. Runs A and B said so and guessed at the intended wording; every guess was wrong. Run C did not notice.

title: Structure
section: Run C is the one to look at
text:
Run C is the one to look at
Runs A and B are what a frontier model does on two passages, and they did well. Run C is the affordable model, the one the Tropical project uses across 53,000 articles, on the same passages (notes). It attributed the editor’s headnote to Agar (“confirms the tree sketched for Dr. Trimen was an undoubted Ledgeriana”), reported the damaged OCR sentence as fact, and dropped the hedges (“I believe”, “some of these trees”). Its output reads well. The review step in the next pages exists for run C. (The same model with its reasoning mode on spent sixteen minutes and 24,000 tokens deliberating about the format and produced no records at all.)

title: Structure
text:
Agent versus model
Two different things happened here. A coding agent read the files, wrote and ran a Python script, and saved outputs. An extraction model (the same model, in this case, reading the text) decided what the records were. In a larger project the script the agent writes will call a model for each chunk, apply ordinary code for the rest, and look things up in external services. When you inspect a result you should be able to tell which of those produced it.
Next: Ground.

title: Clean, together
text:
The OCR for this corpus is Chandra 2, a vision-language model. It was tested on the collection and performs well. Here is what it wrote for the last paragraphs of Agar’s letter, and what the page says:







Chandra 2
The page




… and were now in a full condition and in flower.
… and were growing in a bad situation and not robust.


I have by my prints of the leaves of some of the trees as well as the other that Mr. Moens had sent to be true Ledgerianas …
I have many plants from the seed of the specimen tree as well as the others that Mr. Moens declared to be true Ledgerianas …



Open the scan, right-hand column, last three paragraphs. The three readings side by side, including the old archive.org text layer, are in the source pack.
Three things to say about this in the room:

The page is clean and easy to read. This is not a recognition failure. The language model inside the OCR model wrote a different sentence, and because it is a language model, the sentence reads well.
Chandra itself reads the page correctly. Re-run three times on the archive.org page image, one page at a time, it got both sentences right every time (output). The production corpus was OCR’d from the volume PDF in large batches. The error belongs to that run, not to the model’s reading of the page, which is both reassuring and a warning: the same model gives different text under different conditions, and nothing in the text tells you which you got.
The old OCR got it right, noisily. “ami were growing; in a bad situation and not robust.” Its errors look like errors. The new OCR’s errors read like prose. OCR is better than it was, and not perfect.
The frontier models noticed and could not fix it; the affordable model did not notice. Runs A and B flagged these sentences as uncertain and guessed (“in full bloom”, “the others that Moens had said”); every guess was wrong. Run C, the Qwen model the project uses at scale, reported “in a full condition and in flower” as fact. A model may tell you a sentence reads oddly. Only the page tells you what it says.

text:

title: Clean, together
text:
The decision
Reject the reading. Record the corrected transcription with the scan as its source. Keep the OCR as delivered beside it, so the two can be compared, and so the record of what the model saw is honest.
That is case R3 in the exercise.

title: Clean, together
text:
What the correction becomes
One corrected sentence is worth little. The reason for the correction is worth a lot, because it tells the model what to look for across the collection. The prompt:

This example is wrong for the following historical reason: [explain]. Find other records that might have the same problem. Propose a correction and show which records it would affect. After we review the change, rerun a small batch and show both corrected cases and previously accepted cases that changed.

From this page, three rules follow:

An uncertain reading is not data until someone has looked at the page.
A model’s guess at the intended wording is not a reading.
Where two OCRs disagree on a sentence, send it to a human, or re-OCR the page on its own. The archive.org text layer and the production Chandra text disagree exactly where the latter is wrong, so a cheap comparison would flag these places across 63,000 pages, and a second Chandra pass on the flagged pages fixed this one.

Two larger examples of a correction becoming a rule, from the Tropical pipeline, are in What a correction becomes. They are for afterwards.

title: Further: connecting collections
text:
With a supported identity for Henry Trimen, the small dataset from the 1883 dispute connects to the two larger structured collections. outputs/06-connect/henry-trimen-across-collections.json holds the records.
Three things to say about this table in the room.
The links are automated. The Tropical pipeline’s link to Wikidata and to the Colonial Office List were made by rules. No human decision has been recorded for either. For Trimen the evidence is strong enough that the review will be quick. That is not the general case.
Agreement is not independence. The Tropical pipeline also matches profiles to the Colonial Office List graph, and that graph carries its own Wikidata links for many people. When both agree on a QID it is reassuring, but the second source may have inherited the identifier from the first.
The count is not an occurrence count. 863 is the number of chunk-level extracted records. The extraction asks for one representative mention per distinct person per chunk. The 1944 end date is a retrospective article, not a sign of life.

title: Further: connecting collections
text:
The namesakes
The pipeline correctly keeps Henry apart from his brother Roland Trimen (profile P001512, Q932702, also in the Colonial Office List). It also produced two tiny profiles that no Trimen ever bore:








Profile
Printed form
What the scan actually says




P010214 “J. L. Trimen”
“THE LETTER OF ALL THE BARK ALKALOIDS OF THE BURDEKIN DELTA BY J. L. TRIMEN, F.R.S.” (August 1883, p. 88)
“THE EFFECT OF ALTITUDE ON THE ALKALOID OF RED BARK … By J. E. HOWARD, F.R.S.”


P010783 “L. J. L. Trimen”
“confirmed by Mr. L. J. L. Trimen, who certainly ought to be the best authority as to what is and what is not C. Ledyriana” (October 1883, p. 272)
“confirmed by Mr. Ledger himself, who certainly ought to be the best authority as to what is and what is not C. Ledgeriana”



Both were checked against the page images on 6 October 2026. They are OCR phantoms: the people are John Eliot Howard and Charles Ledger. The pipeline did the right thing in not merging them into Henry; it could not know they were not people at all. Rare, oddly formed names in a profile table are worth a look at the page before they are kept, linked or counted.

title: Further: connecting collections
text:
What the connection enables
From Trimen’s dispute the network opens outward: Howard and Moens; the planters Christie and Agar; McIvor and Ledger as sources of seed; Peradeniya, Kew and the Java plantations; Howards and Sons as the industrial consumer of the bark. The correspondence catalogue adds Thiselton-Dyer, Daniel Morris and Roland. The research packet holds these as candidate links with their evidence, all still awaiting review. None of it is required for the hour; all of it is where the question goes next.
Next: Your own data.
